nameStory: The racket-tailed emerald gets its name from the distinctive club-shaped widening at the tip of its abdomen, which looks remarkably like the head of an old-fashioned tennis racket or badminton racquet. The 'emerald' part comes from its beautiful metallic green body that shimmers like a precious gemstone in the sunlight.
description: The racket-tailed emerald is a medium-sized dragonfly with a stunning metallic green body that gleams in the sun. This slender hunter has clear, transparent wings and jet-black legs that contrast beautifully with its jewel-toned body. You'll notice fine brown hairs covering parts of its body, giving it a slightly fuzzy texture. Like all dragonflies, it's a skilled aerial predator that catches mosquitoes and other small insects on the wing.

idTips.label: Racket-shaped tail
idTips.description: The abdomen widens noticeably at the very tip, creating a distinctive club or racket shape that's visible even in flight

idTips.label: Metallic green body
idTips.description: The thorax and abdomen shine with a brilliant metallic green color that shifts and gleams as the dragonfly moves in different light

idTips.label: Black legs
idTips.description: All six legs are entirely black, appearing almost lacquered and contrasting sharply with the bright green body

idTips.label: Clear wings
idTips.description: Wings are completely transparent with no colored patches, allowing you to see through them easily

idTips.label: Brown body hair
idTips.description: Look closely and you'll see fine brown hairs covering parts of the body, giving it a slightly fuzzy appearance rather than completely smooth

habitat: Racket-tailed emeralds prefer wooded ponds, slow-moving streams, and boggy areas surrounded by trees. They're often found near acidic waters like those in pine barrens or mixed forest wetlands. Look for them patrolling sunny clearings near their aquatic breeding sites, especially where there's a good mix of open water and overhanging vegetation.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from their aquatic larval stage in late spring, but they're not yet at peak numbers. Fresh emeralds may appear less vibrant as their colors haven't fully developed.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season when adults are most active and numerous. This is the best time to spot them patrolling their territories and engaging in mating flights over suitable water bodies.
seasonality.fall: Numbers decline significantly as the flying season winds down. Any remaining adults become increasingly sluggish as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: No adults present - they overwinter as larvae (nymphs) underwater, slowly developing in the muddy bottoms of ponds and streams.

funFact: Racket-tailed emerald larvae can actually shoot water out of their rear ends like tiny jet engines to escape predators - this hydraulic propulsion system can launch them several inches instantly through the water!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with its smaller cousin, the petite emerald, which has a similar metallic green body. The key difference is that the petite emerald lacks the distinctive racket-shaped tail widening - its abdomen tapers to a normal point. Remember: 'racket tail = racket-tailed emerald.'
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the petite emerald, the racket-tailed emerald is larger and has that unmistakable club-shaped tail tip that gives it its name. The petite emerald has a similar metallic green color and black legs, but its abdomen narrows to a typical pointed tip rather than widening into a racket shape. Both species share the same clear wings and fine body hairs, making the tail shape your best distinguishing feature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Petite Emerald is smaller and more delicate than its cousin the Racket-tailed Emerald, which has distinctive club-shaped appendages at the tip of its abdomen that look like tiny tennis rackets.
